Teriflunomide-driven differentiation of uridine-salvage-low AML

Hypothesis. In primary AML with a differentiation blockade and low functional uridine salvage, teriflunomide at clinically attainable unbound exposure will inhibit DHODH-dependent pyrimidine synthesis, induce durable myeloid differentiation, and reduce leukemia-initiating capacity while preserving normal hematopoietic progenitor function. Candidate facts requiring verification—unverified prior knowledge—are that teriflunomide is approved for relapsing multiple sclerosis and inhibits DHODH, the dihydroorotate-to-orotate enzyme in de novo pyrimidine synthesis. The packet does not verify these drug-specific facts, its current label, or relevant human exposure.

Supported premises. DHODH inhibition promoted differentiation and affected disease-related endpoints in experimental AML systems [S4]. This supports investigating the pathway, not assuming that teriflunomide reproduces those results. Differentiation, bulk-cell killing, and stem-cell elimination must remain separate outcomes. The ROS-low, BCL-2-associated leukemia-stem-cell dependency described in S1 does not establish a general mitochondrial therapeutic window [S1]. Cytarabine-residual cells in S2 displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated features without consistent leukemia-stem-cell enrichment [S2]. Venetoclax–azacitidine provides an established metabolic comparator, not the proposed repurposing discovery [S3].

Speculative bridges. Limited uridine salvage is predicted to make some AML samples unusually dependent on de novo pyrimidine synthesis. The central conjecture is that partial, sustained nucleotide restriction can produce maturation before nonspecific toxicity in this context. Neither salvage-low enrichment, a differentiation-selective exposure window, nor preservation of normal progenitors is established by the packet. Reduced leukemia-initiating activity is a further predicted consequence of durable maturation, not something inferred from differentiation markers alone.

Alternative explanations. Apparent differentiation could reflect preferential killing of immature cells, transient cell-cycle arrest, or an off-target drug effect. Extracellular uridine could bypass the proposed dependency. Normal progenitors might share it, eliminating selectivity. Baseline salvage measurements could also correlate with proliferation rather than identify the causal vulnerability.

Discriminating preclinical strategy. First verify approval, indication, biochemical target activity, and human unbound exposure independently. Establish exposure-bounded concentration–time experiments using measured free drug and independently verified plasma-relevant protein and uridine conditions; avoid artificially pyrimidine-depleted medium. Prospectively classify primary AML samples by isotope-traced uridine contribution to nucleotide synthesis, with prespecified salvage-low and salvage-high strata. Include healthy-donor CD34-positive progenitors, vehicle controls, genetic DHODH suppression as a mechanistic comparator, and venetoclax–azacitidine as an established treatment benchmark. Assess whether salvage status predicts response after accounting for baseline proliferation.

Measure biochemical DHODH inhibition, early dihydroorotate accumulation, and nucleotide-pool changes before assessing maturation, proliferation, and apoptosis over several days. Use morphology and lineage-marker changes in tracked viable cells to distinguish genuine maturation from selective survival. Test supplemental uridine rescue only after demonstrating uptake and restoration of nucleotide pools: rescue of both metabolic changes and differentiation would support pyrimidine restriction as the mediator. Genetic DHODH suppression should reproduce the relevant phenotype. If technically feasible, a biochemically validated drug-resistant DHODH construct would provide stronger drug–target attribution; its availability is not assumed.

After washout, quantify clonogenic recovery and conduct limiting-dilution xenotransplantation with equal viable-cell inputs, while separately reporting total surviving-cell burden. This separates durable loss of leukemia-initiating activity from immediate cytotoxicity. Evaluate normal-progenitor multilineage colony output and longer-term repopulating function. Advance to treated xenografts only if measured marrow exposure can reproduce the ex vivo mechanistic window.

Falsifying outcome and limitations. The hypothesis would be falsified if exposure-achievable DHODH blockade and nucleotide depletion produce only transient arrest or apoptosis, without maturation of tracked viable salvage-low cells or durable reduction in leukemia-initiating activity. Dependence on excessive exposure, or comparable impairment of normal progenitors, would refute its translational-selectivity component. AML heterogeneity, changing salvage capacity, niche-provided metabolites, and xenograft effects on homing limit interpretation. Even a positive result would establish a preclinical, context-dependent mechanism—not clinical efficacy or a new established AML regimen.

This effect will occur within independently verified clinically attainable unbound exposure limits and spare normal hematopoietic progenitors sufficiently to provide a preclinical therapeutic window.

Supported premises. DHODH inhibition promoted differentiation and affected disease-related endpoints in experimental AML systems [S4]. This supports investigating the pathway, but does not establish teriflunomide efficacy, achievable exposure, or selectivity. Metabolic vulnerability also need not imply one universal AML compartment: S1 identified oxidative-phosphorylation dependence in studied quiescent leukemia stem cells, whereas cytarabine-resistant cells in S2 were not consistently enriched for that population [S1, S2]. Accordingly, differentiation, bulk-cell survival, and leukemia-propagating function must be measured separately. Teriflunomide is approved for relapsing multiple sclerosis and inhibits DHODH; DHODH catalyzes dihydroorotate-to-orotate conversion in de novo pyrimidine synthesis; uridine salvage can bypass this pathway. The speculative bridges are that teriflunomide can reproduce the differentiation phenotype reported for DHODH inhibition, that weak salvage predicts susceptibility under marrow-relevant conditions, and that normal progenitors retain sufficient metabolic flexibility to tolerate the same exposure. The central causal chain is falsified if exposure-bounded treatment demonstrably engages DHODH and depletes pyrimidines in prospectively classified low-salvage AML, yet fails to induce genuine differentiation or reduce leukemia-propagating activity after washout. Activity restricted to supra-achievable exposure, or comparable impairment of normal progenitors, rejects the proposed therapeutic window even if the pathway mechanism operates.
